summary: Extends RSVP-TE to support path keys, which stand in for hidden path segments when paths are computed across multiple domains by cooperating PCEs. It lets setup signaling work without revealing the details of other domains.

eli5.summary: A path key is a token for a hidden part of a route. This note teaches the signaling messages to understand these tokens so connections can still be set up.

subtitle: How RSVP-TE carries a sealed 'path key' in place of a hidden stretch of route when an LSP crosses several domains.

tldr.problem: When a label switched path crosses several domains, each domain's path computation element may not want to reveal the nodes and links inside its domain, yet the signaling that sets up the path needs a route to follow.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5553 defines two Path Key Subobjects (one with a 32-bit PCE-ID, one with a 128-bit PCE-ID) that can sit in an RSVP-TE Explicit Route Object or Record Route Object. A border router later asks the named PCE to expand the key into the real hidden segment.
tldr.outcome: Inter-domain TE LSPs can be signaled without disclosing the internals of a domain. The RFC adds new error values for failed expansions and leaves the policy choices to each operator.

today: RFC 5553 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It works together with RFC 5520, which defines the PCEP side of the path key.

sections.title: Hiding Part of a Path
sections.content:
MPLS and GMPLS Traffic Engineering LSPs are signaled with RSVP-TE (RFC 3209, RFC 3473). Their routes may be computed by Path Computation Elements (PCEs, RFC 4655). When the LSP crosses several domains, such as Autonomous Systems, several PCEs may cooperate, each computing one segment.

To keep the topology inside each AS private, PCEP (RFC 5440) lets a PCE hide a segment, called a Confidential Path Segment (CPS), by encoding it as a Path Key Subobject (PKS) (RFC 5520). RFC 5553 covers the other half of the story: how the PKS is carried in RSVP-TE Explicit Route Objects (EROs) and Record Route Objects (RROs).
sections.eli5: Some networks do not want to tell outsiders exactly which roads they use inside. They hand out a coded ticket instead. This note explains how that ticket travels with the connection request.

sections.title: A Two-AS Usage Scenario
sections.content:
The RFC walks through a network of two ASes. The ingress router in AS-1 wants an LSP to the egress in AS-2. The ingress acts as a Path Computation Client and asks its PCE (PCE-1). PCE-1 can see inside AS-1 but not AS-2, so it cooperates with PCE-2.

PCE-2 does not want to share the path across AS-2, so it reports that stretch as a PKS. PCE-1 returns the full path to the ingress with the AS-2 part still hidden. The ingress signals the LSP with RSVP-TE and puts the path, PKS included, in the ERO.

When the Path message reaches ASBR-2, that router consults PCE-2 to decode the PKS. The information PCE-2 needs is encoded inside the PKS itself. The PKS in the ERO is then replaced with the expanded path segment. The RFC notes that PCE-2 may in some cases sit on ASBR-2 itself.
sections.eli5: The first town draws the map up to the border. The second town only writes a coded ticket for its own stretch. At the border, a local guide reads the ticket and fills in the real roads.

sections.title: The Path Key Subobject
sections.content:
The PKS is a fixed-length subobject of the ERO, holding a Path Key and a PCE-ID. The Path Key is a token that stands for the CPS within the context of the PCE named by the PCE-ID. The PCE-ID identifies the PCE that can decode the key, via a reachable IPv4 or IPv6 address. Usually it is the same PCE that computed the key.

Two variants exist. With an IPv4-sized PCE-ID the subobject Length is always 8. With an IPv6-sized (128-bit) PCE-ID it is always 20. The L bit SHOULD NOT be set, so the subobject is a strict hop.

The PCE-ID MUST be unique within the scope of the domain that the CPS crosses and MUST be understood by the LSR that will act as PCC for the expansion. Its interpretation is domain-local policy. It MAY be a reachable address of the PCE, or a value with no meaning outside the domain (such as a Router ID) to increase security.
sections.eli5: The ticket has a number and the name of the one office that can read it. It also says it must be followed exactly, without skipping any stops.

sections.title: Processing a PKS in an ERO
sections.content:
Ordinary ERO processing from RFC 3209 is unchanged. A PKS must be immediately preceded by a subobject that identifies its head end, such as an incoming interface or node ID. If the first subobject of the ERO in a Path message is a PKS, the LSR MUST send a PathErr with "Routing Problem" / "Bad initial subobject".

If an LSR strips all local subobjects and the next one is a PKS, it MUST try to resolve it into a CPS. It can contact the PCE named in the PKS over PCEP, contact any cooperating PCE, or use the key to index a CPS the originating PCE gave it earlier. The path fragment SHOULD replace the PKS in the ERO.

  • PCE-ID does not match a PCE: PathErr "Routing Problem" with new value 31, Unknown PCE-ID for PKS expansion.
  • PCE cannot be reached: value 32, Unreachable PCE for PKS expansion.
  • PCE cannot decode the key, perhaps because it expired: value 33, Unknown Path Key for PKS expansion.
  • Decoding refused for policy reasons: "Policy Control Failure" / "Inter-domain policy failure".
  • Expanded ERO makes the Path message too large: the LSR MAY replace parts with loose hops or a further PKS; otherwise it MUST send value 34, ERO too large for MTU.

An LSR that does not recognize the subobject reacts as RFC 3209 says, with "Routing Problem" / "Bad Explicit Route Object".
sections.eli5: When the border guide sees a ticket, they ask the right office to read it. If the office is unknown, unreachable, or the ticket is too old, the guide sends back a note saying why.

sections.title: Path Keys in Record Route Objects
sections.content:
The Record Route Object records the route an LSP actually took. At a domain boundary, the segment to be hidden MAY be replaced in the RRO with a PKS, which can be more useful for diagnostics than the raw route.

On a Resv message the PKS used SHOULD be the one originally signaled in the ERO. On a Path message the PKS SHOULD identify the LSR doing the replacing and give a key that can expand the segment. In that case the LSR SHOULD keep the key and its expansion for at least the lifetime of the LSP, and make the expansion available to diagnostic tools under local policy. Hiding RRO segments needs to be configurable, and the default is to hide nothing.
sections.eli5: The trip diary can also use the sticker for private stretches. The border guide keeps the real answer on file so repair crews can look it up later if allowed.

sections.title: Security and Probing Risks
sections.content:
The exchanges are point-to-point and can be authenticated and secured with standard PCEP and RSVP-TE techniques. The RFC adds that the PCE providing an expansion is RECOMMENDED to check that the requester is the head end of the resulting CPS. A PCE-ID that only means something inside the domain gives further protection.

The listed concerns are: probing a PCE for expansions of random keys, deducing information from detailed error codes, a forged or altered Path Key leading to a wrong ERO, and denial of service. An LSR worried about leaking information through errors MAY report every failure as "Policy Control Failure" / "Inter-domain policy failure". A flood of Path messages with spurious PKSs is countered by RSVP-TE integrity protection and its chain-of-trust model.
sections.eli5: Nobody should be able to guess ticket numbers and learn the secret roads. So the office only answers the router that is really at the start of that stretch.

sections.title: IANA Allocations
sections.content:
IANA allocated two new subobject types, used in both the EXPLICIT_ROUTE object (Class Number 20) and the ROUTE_RECORD object (Class Number 21): 64 for a Path Key with a 32-bit PCE-ID and 65 for a Path Key with a 128-bit PCE-ID. These are the same numbers RFC 5520 uses for the PKS in PCEP.

Under the "Routing Problem" error code (24), IANA allocated error values 31 to 34 as listed in the processing rules.
sections.eli5: The registry keeper gave the tickets their own official numbers and added four new reasons for sending a complaint note.
